text: Have them bring a young bull and a grain offering of choice flour moistened with olive oil, along with a second young bull for a sin offering.

content:
We have walked through the cleansing of the Levites; the water, the razor,
the washed garments. We stood at the altar and watched two bulls being prepared; the sin offering & the burnt offering. Yesterday we saw how both of those offerings found their perfect fulfilment in Christ, whose consecrated life began at his baptism and was completed at Calvary. Today we come to something different; something quieter in appearance, but no less deep in meaning. Alongside the first bull, the burnt offering, a grain offering was brought: choice flour moistened with olive oil. No blood. No sacrifice of life. Just flour and oil. And yet Yahweh required it. He placed it there deliberately, side by side with the burnt offering, as another layer of the portrait He was painting. Today we look carefully at what that grain offering was telling us; about the One it was pointing to all along.

The first thing we are told about this grain offering is that the flour was choice flour; in Hebrew, soleth. This was not ordinary household flour. It was wheat flour, not barley. It was carefully sifted, finely ground, the highest quality available. When you held it in your hand there were no lumps, no rough patches, no unground portions. Every part of it had been through the grinding process completely. It was uniform, pure, and consistent throughout.

This is a picture of the perfect humanity of Christ. His character was not uneven. He was not patient in one moment and harsh the next. He was not holy in public and compromised when no one was watching. He was not tender with some people and cruel with others. His character was, in every part, like that fine flour; uniform, consistent, without a single moral lump or blemish anywhere. The testing He went through in this life was itself the grinding process, and every time He came through it, what remained was choice flour. Every trial pressed against Him. Every temptation ground at Him.
Every opposition came from a different direction. And the result was always the same purity. Consistency. The same character on the inside as on the outside. John writes simply: "In him is no sin" (1 John 3:5). The writer of Hebrews confirms: "He was in all points tested as we are, yet without sin" (Hebrews 4:15). Every grain crushed and grounded; and what came out was always choice flour. No impurity was ever found in Him.

And the flour contained no leaven. This detail matters enormously. Throughout Scripture, leaven consistently represents sin, corruption, and false teaching.
Its very nature is to spread and work through whatever it touches invisibly, puffing up what ought to be flat. Yahweh commanded that no leaven be found in the grain offering (Leviticus 2:11). This was not incidental; it was a declaration of what the offering represented. In Christ there was no corruption at work, no hidden sin spreading through what appeared clean on the surface, no moral leaven of any kind. "He made him who knew no sin to be sin for us" (2 Corinthians 5:21); the very fact that our sin had to be laid on him from outside confirms that none of it originated from within him. The flour was without leaven. The man was without sin.

The flour was not dry. This is where the grain offering becomes especially beautiful. The flour was moistened; soaked through - with olive oil.
Not drizzled on top. Not lightly brushed. The word carries the sense of the oil being worked into the flour, permeating it, so that every part of the flour was touched by the oil. And olive oil throughout Scripture is the consistent symbol of the Ruach HaKodesh; the Spirit of Yahweh. From the anointing of kings and priests to the oil that kept the lampstand burning through the night, olive oil speaks of divine anointing, divine enabling, the presence of the Spirit at work.

Christ was not a man who received the Spirit occasionally, for specific tasks, and then operated on his own in between. He was anointed without measure; the Spirit was poured upon him and through him entirely, as the oil permeated every part of the flour. At his baptism, the Spirit descended upon him and remained (John 1:32-33). Peter declared it plainly in Acts 10:38: "God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power." Every healing, every teaching, every act of authority, every moment of compassion, every night of prayer; all of it was Spirit-moistened. There was no dry portion in the flour,
no part of his life where the oil had not reached. The Spirit was not a supplement to his ministry; but was the oil that made the whole offering cohesive, fragrant, and fit to be presented to Yahweh.

Now flour and oil together tell us something that is both profound and deeply personal for us. Acts 2:22 describes Christ as "a man approved of God"; not God appearing as a man, but a man, a real human being, confirmed and empowered by Yahweh. The grain offering says the same thing: perfect humanity, fully Spirit-anointed. He did not live his life drawing on resources that were unavailable to us. He lived it as a Spirit-filled man; obedient, yielded, dependent on the Father, which is exactly why his life can be the pattern for ours. The fine flour shows us what we are called to become. The oil shows us how it is possible. And together they show us what it looks like when a human life is wholly given over to Yahweh.

There is one more dimension of the grain offering we must not pass over.
The grain was not simply found lying in the wilderness. It had to be grown.
A farmer had to prepare the ground, sow the seed, wait through the seasons, gather the harvest, thresh the grain, and then grind it into flour. The grain offering was the fruit of deliberate, patient, costly human labor; the earth yielding what was in it through long and careful work, then that fruit being offered back to Yahweh. This is why the grain offering spoke of dedication, thanksgiving, and the labor of human hands returned to the One who gave the ground and the rain in the first place.

In the same way, Christ’s life of dedicated service to Yahweh was not effortless. It was not easy or automatic. Hebrews 5:8 tells us that "he learned obedience through the things he suffered." Every step from Nazareth to Golgotha was a step of intentional, costly dedication to his Father's will. The ground was prepared at his baptism. The seed was sown through thirty years of quiet, hidden obedience in a household in Galilee. It grew through three and half years of ministry; through rejection, misunderstanding, weariness, temptation, and the pressure of those who hated him. It was threshed in Gethsemane, where he sweat drops of blood and said "not my will, but yours." And the harvest came at Calvary, where he could say with a full heart: "It is finished." The grain offering says that none of this happened by accident. It was the fruit of a life wholly, deliberately, at every stage directed toward Yahweh. That is what was being presented on the altar. Not a single moment of sacrifice but a lifetime of sacrifice.

When the grain offering was presented, the priest did not burn all of it. He took a handful; called the memorial portion and burned it on the altar. The smoke ascended to Yahweh as a sweet aroma, a reminder before the Father of the dedication being offered. The rest of the grain offering was not wasted.
It became food for Aaron and his sons the priests ate from it. It became their provision, their daily sustenance, their living from the offering that had been presented.

Both portions speak to us of Christ. The memorial portion burning on the altar and ascending as a sweet aroma before Yahweh points to what Paul declares in Ephesians 5:2: "Christ also has loved us and given himself for us, an offering and a sacrifice to God for a sweet-smelling aroma." His sacrifice did not disappear into the past. It ascends eternally before the Father; a memorial before Yahweh that never grows cold, never fades, never needs to be repeated. The smoke is still rising. And the priests' portion, the remainder that the priests lived from points to what Christ said in John 6:57: "He who eats me will live because of me." The priests lived from the grain offering. We live from Christ. His life, his obedience, his perfect humanity, his Spirit-filled walk; these are not just things we admire from a distance. They are what we feed on. They sustain us. They become our provision for the life Yahweh has called us to live.

When we step back and look at the whole picture, we see how perfectly the grain offering completes what the two bulls began. The sin offering dealt with our guilt. The burnt offering declared total consecration. And now the grain offering says: and here is what that consecrated life actually looked like in the living of it. Fine flour, a perfectly consistent, sinless character, ground through every trial without a single lump of impurity. No leaven no corruption of any kind, ever, anywhere. Olive oil soaking through every part a life lived entirely in the power and anointing of the Spirit, not a single moment dry. And the fruit of costly, patient, deliberate labor thirty-three and half years of ground prepared, seed sown, and harvest brought in, every step directed toward the Father.

This is what was laid on the altar at Calvary. Not just a sin-bearing transaction; though that it was, fully and finally. But the offering of a whole life: choice, pure, anointed, labored-over, fragrant. A life that had never been anything other than fully given to Yahweh. And that memorial portion still ascends before the Father even now; and we, like the priests, live from what was offered. The offering feeds us. The obedience sustains us. The Spirit-anointed humanity of Christ becomes the pattern and the provision for our own walk before Yahweh. One grain offering. One Christ. Everything covered. Everything provided.

title: Prayer
text:
O Yahweh, our God,

The more we look at what You prepared in the wilderness camp,

the more we are undone by the depth of what You were showing us.

Fine flour; no impurity, no unevenness, ground through every trial and still pure.

Oil that soaked through, no dry place, the Spirit filling everything.

The labor of the years, nothing accidental, everything pictured toward Christ.

And then the memorial portion ascending; still before You, still fragrant, still accepted.

We thank You that we do not merely admire this offering from a distance but,

we are invited to live from it, to eat from it, to be sustained by it daily.

Let the fine flour of his perfect life be the pattern we walk toward.

Let the oil of his anointing remind us what we too have been given.

And let the costly labor of his obedience teach us that our own dedication

must also be grown through patience, pressed through suffering, and wholly given to You.

Great is Yahweh and greatly to be praised;

His greatness is unsearchable. Psalm 145:3

We ask this in the name of the choice flour and the anointed One, our Christ.

Amen.
